rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and critical pairs while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to identify which critical pairs respond to slope, especially the late coeluting cluster. This diagnostic run will show whether shallowing the gradient improves selectivity enough to justify a narrower gradient window.

The late coelution barely responded to gradient slope, so test temperature-dependent selectivity using the original gradient. Higher temperature may separate that cluster while keeping the final peak below 10 minutes.

Probe the low-temperature endpoint because heating worsened the early critical pair without resolving the late cluster. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature selectivity and should leave the final peak near the 10-minute threshold.

Raise the starting organic fraction to remove unused weak-solvent time while making the gradient shallower. This should improve slope-sensitive late pairs without the time penalty of simply lengthening the original gradient.

Further narrow and shallow the gradient to improve the unresolved late pairs while using the time saved by a higher starting organic fraction. Monitor the early peaks for compression as the starting strength increases.

Test whether a higher starting fraction and shallower gradient can improve the stubborn late cluster while retaining a sub-10-minute last peak. This also probes whether the early pair compressed in injection 6 crosses and separates again.

Refine the best method with a slightly shallower gradient, targeting the middle unresolved pairs and improved late-cluster resolution. Retain the 0.30 starting fraction to avoid the early-pair compression seen at 0.40.

Test temperature selectivity around the improved gradient rather than the original broad window. A modest increase should remove the small time penalty and reveal whether the remaining middle and late pairs improve or deteriorate.

Test a slightly lower starting fraction to preserve middle-pair selectivity while keeping a relatively shallow gradient. This brackets the best starting window and will show whether improved resolution offsets any small time penalty.

Probe a shallower gradient at an intermediate starting fraction, aiming to improve the late cluster while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. The key tradeoff is whether middle-pair resolution remains adequate as the starting organic fraction increases.

Test a hold-based alternative by ending the gradient near the late cluster’s elution strength. The stubborn coelution has barely responded to slope or temperature; moving it into the final hold probes a different selectivity regime, although the last peak may incur a time penalty.

Return to a gradient-based method with a lower starting fraction and a slope between injections 5 and 10. This targets full resolution of the middle pairs while keeping the final peak close to 10 minutes.

Bracket the temperature optimum around injection 8 with a single 5 °C increase. This should move the final peak below 10 minutes while testing whether the remaining resolution losses stay small enough to improve CRF.

Test a shortened gradient ending at 0.65, with a slope close to the best-performing methods. The late cluster should remain near the gradient end, while the final hold tests whether the last peaks can still elute within 10 minutes.

Use one exploratory injection to test a substantially different starting window, where compressed middle pairs may change order and separate again. This also checks whether the persistent late coelution responds to stronger initial conditions rather than small slope adjustments.
Return to the best starting window and test a slightly shallower slope than injection 8. This probes whether bringing the middle pair to full resolution outweighs the expected small time penalty.

Test a distinctly steeper gradient to check for a second selectivity optimum after close pairs change elution order. The current shallow-gradient optimum appears limited by a persistent late coelution, so this run explores an alternative while leaving time for final refinement.

Refine the lower-starting-window option with a slightly steeper slope than injection 13 to reduce its time penalty. The target is to retain near-full resolution of the middle pairs while bringing the last peak closer to 10 minutes.

Combine the better-preserved early separation at a 0.25 start with a shallower gradient and moderate heating. This tests whether temperature can offset the added retention time while the shallower slope restores resolution of the middle pairs.
Test whether a 5 °C increase removes injection 17’s time penalty while preserving its improved middle-pair resolution. This is a local refinement near the best-performing gradient window.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 8, with an endpoint high enough to avoid the hold-related delay seen at 0.65. This should keep the final peak below 10 minutes while measuring the resolution cost of shortening the separation.

Check the nearest temperature neighbor of the best-scoring method. A 5 °C increase should keep the final peak comfortably below 10 minutes and tests whether a small selectivity shift improves the overall resolution balance at this starting fraction.

Test the remaining slope bracket at the 0.20 starting fraction, between injections 5 and 13. The slightly steeper gradient should eliminate the time penalty while checking whether the middle pairs retain enough resolution to challenge the best score.

Use the final injection to test a lower starting fraction with a compensating steeper slope, targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. This checks whether preserving middle-pair selectivity at the lower start can outperform the closely matched optima at 0.25 and 0.30.
